description: Neo Genesis is a creative collective born to redefine boundaries and spark inspiration. Blending futuristic aesthetics with immersive storytelling, we design next-generation digital experiences. Step into our universe, where every idea shines like a distant star.
summary:
Neo Universe is an interactive, story-driven website created by Team Neo Genesis. Its main story, Ghost Explorers, brings to life 20 pieces of NASA hardware left behind on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space—some now silent, and some still talking. Across eight chapters, from the birth of NASA in 1958 and the Apollo mirrors of 1969 to Voyager 1 today, these explorers share one enduring mission: go farther, and send what you learn back home.

Designed for kindergarten, primary, and secondary school students, the site adapts to different ages. Young learners can enjoy full-screen animated chapter videos and read-aloud narration where each machine tells its own story in the first person. Older students can dive deeper with an interactive solar system map, a timeline, a hardware comparison tool, and 3D models that explain how each part worked and what science it made possible, reinforced by a recap quiz and achievement badges.

Our project transforms dense NASA mission data into a human story so these abandoned machines are never forgotten—helping young people feel a personal connection to space exploration and inspire them to carry the mission forward.
details:
What does it do?

  • Neo Universe is an interactive website about 20 pieces of NASA hardware left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space.
  • Its main story, Ghost Explorers, has eight chapters and eight generations. It runs from the Apollo mirrors of 1969 to Voyager 1 today.
  • Every chapter carries the same mission: go farther, and send what you learn back home.
  • Each machine tells its own story in the first person, so a silent rover becomes a character.
  • The 20 machines are split into 5 on the Moon, 8 on Mars and 7 in deep space.

How does it work?

  • Story mode: the visitor reads the chapters one by one and can open the machines mentioned in each chapter.
  • Solar system map: planets orbit, the Moon circles Earth, and pins mark where hardware is. Clicking Earth, the Moon, Mars or the outer ring opens a list of the machines there.
  • Timeline: a swipeable carousel that orders the machines by the year they started working.
  • Comparison tool: two machines side by side, with their location, status, working years, power, movement, signal delay and a bar showing how long each one worked.
  • AI chatbot: allow to user to ask other information of the equipment NASA used in space exploration
  • 3D Lab: the visitor drags to rotate a model, scrolls to zoom, and taps a part to see its name and what it did. Voyager, Pioneer, Opportunity, Spirit, InSight, Ingenuity, the Apollo Lunar Module, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler, Viking and Dawn have 3D models.
  • Read aloud: text to speech reads each machine’s story and each part’s description.
  • Videos: each machine links to a short video.
  • Quiz: 10 questions with shuffled answers. Each answer shows a “Did you know?” fact, and the visitor can retry only the missed questions.
  • Mini-games: Memory Match (match pictures to names), Place Sorter (Moon, Mars or deep space?) and Who Am I? (guess the machine from clues).
  • Badges: 12 achievements for opening explorers, reading the story, taking the quiz and playing the games.
  • Progress and best scores are saved in the browser’s local storage.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns dense mission data into a story that children can feel.
  • It covers old, finished missions that school-age learners rarely hear about.
  • It connects each machine’s engineering to the science it made possible, such as marsquakes from InSight, the first flight on another planet from Ingenuity, and the first asteroid landing from NEAR Shoemaker.
  • It works for three age groups: kindergarten children, primary pupils and secondary students.
  • It is free and runs in a normal browser, with no install and no account needed beyond a simple entry page.

What is the intended impact?

  • Children feel a personal connection to the machines and remember them like characters.
  • Students see space exploration as a long, shared mission passed from one generation to the next.
  • Teachers get a classroom-ready tool that mixes reading, data, 3D exploration and games.
  • Young people are inspired to imagine building the next explorer.

What tools, languages and software did we use?

  • Languages and tools:
  • HTML: Website structure.
  • CSS: Styling, responsive layouts and light/dark themes.
  • JavaScript: Interactive controls, image processing and data visualisation.
  • Three.js (r128) for the 3D models, with GLTFLoader for NASA GLB files.
  • SVG for the solar system map and Canvas for the animated starfield.
  • The Web Speech API for read aloud.
  • Local storage for progress, badges and best scores.
  • Node.js and glTF-Transform to convert NASA 3D models (decompress them and shrink the textures) so they run in the browser.
  • Software Platform:
    1.Visual studio code: used to write the code of the website
    2.Puter Ai: Act as an AI chatbot in the website
    3.Firebase: allow us to make an account system

How is it creative?

  • The “ghost” idea turns abandoned hardware into something to remember instead of forget.
  • First-person narration gives each machine a voice.
  • A single mission thread links 68 years of exploration into seven chapters.
  • Twin machines (Voyager 1 and 2, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2) are shown as families.
  • The games reuse the same data, so every game is also a lesson.
  • Glowing hotspots on the 3D models turn learning about parts into exploring.
  • The combination of quiz, mini games, ai chatbot and 3d model make the learning progress is interesting

What factors did our team consider?

  • Age range: simple pictures and read-aloud for younger children, deeper data and 3D parts for older students.
  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA public pages, and we say clearly that the narrations are simplified dramatizations.
  • Accessibility: keyboard-friendly map pins and buttons, labels for screen readers, reduced-motion support, and a layout that works on phones.
  • Performance: detailed 3D models load only when opened, so the first page loads fast.
  • Privacy: progress stays on the user’s own device.
